blocks.content: The status field is the observed current state covered in the Internals module, and it comes with one firm rule: you never hand-write it in a manifest you apply.
1. status Is the Observed State, Formally
blocks.text: 1. status Is the Observed State, Formally

blocks.content: Exactly as covered in the Desired State vs Current State topic, status reflects reality as actually observed by the relevant component, kubelet reporting a Pod's real condition, for instance, not something declared by intention.

blocks.alt: Reality as actually observed, not a declaration of intent, the direct counterpart to spec

blocks.content: 2. Never Hand-Write This in a Manifest You Apply
blocks.text: 2. Never Hand-Write This in a Manifest You Apply

blocks.content: This is a firm, important rule, a manifest you write and apply should never include a status field, it is not yours to declare, it is populated entirely by the system based on real, observed reality.

blocks.alt: A field that never belongs in anything you write and apply yourself

blocks.content: This connects directly to the real API detail covered in the Internals module, status is a genuinely separate subresource with its own RBAC permissions, updating it is a distinct operation from updating spec, reserved for the components actually authorized to report real observations.

blocks.alt: A genuinely separate subresource, with its own distinct permissions, covered in the Internals module

blocks.content: 4. Useful to Read, Never to Declare
blocks.text: 4. Useful to Read, Never to Declare

blocks.content: This is the practical, actionable distinction: reading status (via kubectl get -o yaml, or describe, covered throughout this course) is genuinely useful for understanding real state, writing it yourself is never the right move.

blocks.alt: Genuinely useful to read, never something you should be writing yourself

blocks.content: kubectl get pod my-app -o yaml | grep -A5 "^status:"

code.content: kubectl get pod my-app -o yaml | grep -A5 "^status:"

codes.bash: kubectl get pod my-app -o yaml | grep -A5 "^status:"

blocks.content: pod.status.phase, exactly the field covered in full in the Pod Phases topic, is a perfect concrete example, it reflects real, observed reality (Pending, Running, and so on), and it is never something you would set yourself in a manifest.

blocks.alt: The exact field from the Pod Phases topic, a perfect concrete example of this whole pattern

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: status is the observed current state, managed via its own separate subresource, and it should never appear as something you hand-write in a manifest you apply.
It is genuinely useful to read, kubectl get -o yaml or describe, covered throughout this course, but never something to declare yourself.
